chapter: Band personalities, Duke's last years and the office
title: Al Celley's money handling and character
summary: Willard says Celley charged interest and demanded double receipts, but never made a mistake with money.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, Al Celley used to do a lot of strange things, like collect double receipts and charge interest on loans to the guys in the band.

Paul Gonsalves was always drawing on his salary, and Paul Gonsalves paid the most exorbitant rates of interest to Al Celley you ever heard of. Celley used to ask me to sign double receipts when he paid me -- two receipts; that meant that Celley had accounted for twice as much money as he paid out.

I never will understand about Celley. He always got all the money in his pocket. Like we'd play a dance tonight and he'd get the money and he'd put it in his pocket. I give this man -- Duke Ellington won $50, the
other man would win so and so, Duke Ellington won over $40, and he'd give all that money to everybody, but he didn't keep an account of it.

Well, Al Kelley was not the nicest person in the world, but he did have a brilliant mind and was a great mathematician, and I don't think he had any doubt what he did; I think he knew -- he didn't have to write it down. I think he knew every penny he spent.
Yeah, he had a good mind.
He was a very, very brilliant man.
And he was very nice to me.
The only thing that bothered me was that he was a crook.
And I used to ask Duke, you know, 'Why do you have a crook handling your money?'

We used to room sometimes together, and you know, he'd snore like crazy; you'd hear him for a block! And when we would go out, he would take me to the barbershop and he would say let me take a close shave because you're liable to get run over. (laughter)

And what was so funny was that he would make a lot of mistakes because of his bad vision, except with money -- but he never made a mistake with money. People in the band used to say that he could feel the numbers on the bills, or smell the difference. You know how he would
Yeah, he used to do just like this ...
Well, the guys in the band used to say that he wasn't trying to see the numbers; he was smelling the difference between them.

I stayed in his house in Pennsylvania; we were working at that theatre across from Philadelphia, you know? On a Sunday, I think it was, and after that, he asked me to take him over and drive the car over to Pennsylvania, and I said, 'but I don't know how to get there', and he said, "I'll show you", so he really drove me over there. I mean, I drove the car, but he told me where to go and this and the other. I slept that night over there and we came back the next day.

But it used to be hard to get my money out of him; if I did an extraction or anything like that, I told him I wanted my money, so I used to say I was going to quit, that I was going to get out of there, and then he would always give me whatever I want.
